newsitem.title: CHINA: China interest rate cut in 1997 possible - official.
newsitem.headline: China interest rate cut in 1997 possible - official.

text.p: China could cut interest rates this year with inflation continuing to fall, but the authorities could also decide to use other means to reduce the cost of money, a senior central bank official said on Monday.

Di Weiping, executive vice-president of the People's Bank of China's Shanghai branch, said a thorough reform of the interest rate and bank reserve ratio structure was being considered by the central bank authorities.
If implemented, the reforms could make an interest rate cut unnecessary, he told Reuters in an interview.
"There will probably still be some interest rate cuts because the inflation rate in the first quarter came down further. But there will not necessarily be one," he said.

"The cost of the renminbi (yuan) is not just the interest rate. There may be other measures that could be taken by the central bank to reduce the overall cost of renminbi to commercial banks," he added.

China's monetary authorities cut interest rates twice in 1996, in May and August, and there has been intense speculation in the Chinese financial markets in recent weeks over the possibility of a further cut.
Di said reducing the bank reserve ratios, the proportion of deposits the banks are required to keep in reserve, would have a similar impact to a reduction in the interest rates.
Such a cut has been mooted for nearly a year, but analysts say it has been delayed largely by central bank fears of a surge of money pouring into the economy and fuelling inflation.

"We can further reduce interest rates, or we could take advantage of this current situation to restructure the entire interest rate and deposit reserve structure to make renminbi interest rates more rational and more closely related to demand and supply," Di said.
He said he had no information on when a cut in the reserve ratio might take place or to what degree, adding that no decision has been made.
"But the current monetary policy stance -- moderately tight -- should be continued so as to prevent any possibility of prices rising in the second half of the year," he said.
